claim: There are now over 40 different human amyloid diseases, each linked to the buildup of a specific precursor protein or peptide
source: There are now over 40 different human amyloid diseases, each linked to the buildup of a specific precursor protein or peptide (Chiti and Dobson, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chiti and Dobson, 2009

claim: Mature amyloid fibrils are composed of cross β-sheet structure
source: X-ray fiber diffraction indicates that the insoluble, mature amyloid fibrils are composed of cross β-sheet structure (Jahn et al., 2010; Eisenberg and Jucker, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jahn et al., 2010 and Eisenberg and Jucker, 2012

claim: Soluble oligomeric intermediates, not the insoluble well-ordered fibrils, are preferentially responsible for cellular toxicity
source: Another feature of these diseases is that soluble oligomeric intermediates, not the insoluble well-ordered fibrils, are preferentially responsible for cellular toxicity (Bucciantini et al., 2002; Hardy and Selkoe, 2002; Tomic et al., 2009; Xue et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Bucciantini et al., 2002; Hardy and Selkoe, 2002; Tomic et al., 2009; Xue et al., 2009

claim: The soluble oligomeric forms of the prion protein are the most infectious per unit protein
source: Similarly, the soluble oligomeric forms of the prion protein are the most infectious per unit protein (Silveira et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Silveira et al., 2005

claim: Fibrils may be protective, at least up to a point, as their breakdown to smaller aggregates yields greater toxicity and infectivity
source: As such, fibrils may be protective, at least up to a point, as their breakdown to smaller aggregates yields greater toxicity and infectivity.
evidence: Based on inference from the preceding statement about oligomers being more toxic than fibrils

claim: A compound that promotes inclusion formation while reducing toxicity and cellular pathology supports the hypothesis that fibrils may be protective
source: The discovery of a compound that promotes inclusion formation while reducing toxicity and cellular pathology supports this hypothesis (Bodner et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bodner et al., 2006

claim: Binding the fibrillar state of Aβ could reduce toxicity presumably by shifting the equilibrium from oligomer to fibril
source: In a similar vein, Jiang et al. (2013) demonstrated that binding the fibrillar state of Aβ could reduce toxicity presumably by shifting the equilibrium from oligomer to fibril.
evidence: Supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2013

claim: The soluble oligomer species is more toxic than mature fibrils
source: Research on the soluble oligomers has become critically important since there is a consensus that the soluble oligomer species is more toxic than mature fibrils (Chiti and Dobson, 2006; Tomic et al., 2009; Xue et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citations to Chiti and Dobson, 2006; Tomic et al., 2009; Xue et al., 2009

claim: Fibrils are a reservoir for toxic oligomeric species
source: and, while nontoxic, the fibrils are a reservoir for toxic oligomeric species (Shahnawaz and Soto, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shahnawaz and Soto, 2012

claim: Structural similarities between soluble oligomers from a range of unrelated proteins/peptides has been demonstrated by generation of an antibody that recognizes a common backbone structure
source: In fact, structural similarities between soluble oligomers from a range of unrelated proteins/peptides has been demonstrated by generation of an antibody that recognizes a common backbone structure (Kayed et al., 2003; Tomic et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kayed et al., 2003 and Tomic et al., 2009

claim: The A11 antibody is specific for soluble oligomeric intermediates derived from a variety of peptides and proteins, including Aβ(1-42), α-synuclein, islet amyloid polypeptide, polyglutamine, lysozyme, human insulin, and a prion peptide
source: Glabe and co-workers developed an antibody (denoted A11) that is specific for soluble oligomeric intermediates derived from a variety of peptides and proteins, including Aβ(1-42), α-synuclein, islet amyloid polypeptide, polyglutamine, lysozyme, human insulin, and a prion peptide (Glabe and Kayed, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Glabe and Kayed, 2006

claim: The A11 antibody does not bind the corresponding insoluble fibrils (cross-β structure) or the natively folded precursors
source: The antibody does not, however, bind the corresponding insoluble fibrils (cross-β structure) or the natively folded precursors (various structures).
evidence: Based on inference from the specificity of the A11 antibody described in the context

claim: The A11 antibody inhibits toxicity associated with the intermediates
source: This antibody inhibits toxicity associated with the intermediates, implying a common mechanism of toxicity and offering hope for a broad-based therapeutic agent.
evidence: Based on inference from the discussion of the A11 antibody properties

claim: α-sheet structure is populated during molecular dynamics simulations of a range of amyloid proteins with different structures and sequences under amyloidogenic conditions
source: Some years ago we 'discovered' a novel secondary structure, which we call 'α-sheet', that is populated during molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of a range of amyloid proteins (and peptides) with different structures and sequences under amyloidogenic conditions (Figure 1A) (Armen et al., 2004a, 2004b, 2005; Steward et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Armen et al., 2004a, 2004b, 2005; Steward et al., 2008 and reference to Figure 1A

claim: The position where the α-sheet forms along the sequence coincides with the most amyloidogenic regions of the proteins, as determined experimentally
source: The position where the α-sheet forms along the sequence coincides with the most amyloidogenic regions of the proteins, as determined experimentally (Armen et al., 2004a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Armen et al., 2004a

claim: α-sheet is a common structure involved in the early stages of protein aggregation
source: Consequently, we proposed that α-sheet is a common structure involved in the early stages of protein aggregation (Armen et al., 2004a; Daggett, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Armen et al., 2004a and Daggett, 2006

claim: α-sheet was first predicted by Pauling and Corey and called 'polar pleated sheet'
source: In the course of characterizing the structure observed by MD, we learned that α-sheet was first predicted by Pauling and Corey and called 'polar pleated sheet'.
evidence: Based on historical knowledge of protein structure predictions

claim: Pauling and Corey ruled the α-sheet structure energetically unfavorable and concluded that the β-sheet structure would be favored in normal proteins
source: However, they ruled the structure energetically unfavorable and concluded, correctly, that the β-sheet structure would be favored in normal proteins (Pauling and Corey, 1951).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pauling and Corey, 1951

claim: An α-sheet is similar to a β-sheet, but instead of alternating main chain NH and C = O groups along the strands, an α-sheet has the NH groups aligned on one side and the carbonyls on the other
source: An α-sheet is similar to a β-sheet, but instead of alternating main chain NH and C = O groups along the strands, an α-sheet has the NH groups aligned on one side and the carbonyls on the other.
evidence: Based on structural description of α-sheet

claim: The α-sheet has a molecular dipole and a very different hydrogen-bonding pattern across the sheet compared to a β-sheet
source: As such, the α-sheet has a molecular dipole and a very different hydrogen-bonding pattern across the sheet compared to a β-sheet.
evidence: Based on inference from the structural description of α-sheet

claim: The main chain (Φ, Ψ) dihedral angles of the α-sheet alternate between the αL and αR conformations
source: Interestingly, the main chain (Φ, Ψ) dihedral angles of the α-sheet alternate between the αL and αR conformations (Daggett, 2006) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Daggett, 2006 and reference to Figure 1A

claim: The alternating dihedral angles in α-sheet form an extended chain resulting in the carbonyl groups and amide groups aligning in a plane
source: Although locally helical, the alternating dihedral angles form an extended chain resulting in the carbonyl groups and amide groups aligning in a plane.
evidence: Based on structural description of α-sheet

claim: The alignment of carbonyl and amide groups in α-sheet creates uniform electrostatic faces to aid in the addition of further strands
source: Such an arrangement creates uniform electrostatic faces to aid in the addition of further strands (Armen et al., 2004b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Armen et al., 2004b

claim: A simple peptide plane flip could convert the α-sheet into a β-sheet and ultimately a mature fibril
source: Once a sheet is formed, a simple peptide plane flip could convert the α-sheet into a β-sheet and ultimately a mature fibril (Daggett, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Daggett, 2006

claim: α-sheet structure has been observed in a peptide crystal structure
source: α-sheet structure has been observed in a peptide crystal structure (Di Blasio et al., 1994)
evidence: Supported by citation to Di Blasio et al., 1994

claim: Short stretches of α-strand are present in various proteins in the Protein Data Bank
source: and short stretches of α-strand are present in various proteins in the Protein Data Bank (Daggett, 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to Daggett, 2006

claim: Extensive α-sheet formation has not been observed in native proteins
source: although extensive α-sheet formation has not been observed in native proteins.
evidence: Based on knowledge of protein structures

claim: L-alanine has a conformational preference to adopt the αR conformation
source: Intrinsic residue propensities for L- and D-alanine were calculated from 100 ns of MD simulations of a GGXGG peptide system (Beck et al., 2008) (D-alanine was simulated using the same protocol). The backbone structure (upper panels) as well as the Ramachandran plot of the conformation of the alanine residue during the entire simulation, demonstrate the conformational preference for L-alanine to adopt the αR conformation
evidence: Supported by citation to Beck et al., 2008 and reference to Figure 1B showing MD simulation data

claim: D-alanine has a conformational preference to favor the αL conformation
source: and for D-alanine to favor the αL conformation (lower panels).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1B showing MD simulation data

claim: Peptides containing alternating D- and L-amino acids have previously been shown to form extended structures
source: Peptides containing alternating D- and L-amino acids have previously been shown to form extended structures (De Santis et al., 1974; Heitz et al., 1981)
evidence: Supported by citations to De Santis et al., 1974 and Heitz et al., 1981

claim: Peptides with alternating D- and L-amino acids populate similar conformational space as MD-identified α-sheet sequences consisting solely of L-amino acids
source: and they populate similar conformational space as our MD-identified α-sheet sequences consisting solely of L-amino acids.
evidence: Based on inference from the structural properties of alternating D- and L-amino acid peptides

claim: Both transthyretin and beta amyloid 1-42 have well characterized aggregation profiles and aggregate under mild, non-denaturing conditions
source: Both systems have well characterized aggregation profiles and aggregate under mild, non-denaturing conditions (Quintas et al., 1997; Foss et al., 2005; Hopping et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Quintas et al., 1997; Foss et al., 2005; Hopping et al., 2013

claim: β-hairpins are known inhibitors of Aβ aggregation
source: β-hairpins are known inhibitors of Aβ aggregation (Yamin et al., 2009; Cheng et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yamin et al., 2009 and Cheng et al., 2012

claim: α1 resulted in 72% inhibition of TTR aggregation at 48 hr
source: At these concentrations, α1 and α3 resulted in 72 and 56% inhibition, respectively, relative to TTR alone at low pH.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A

claim: α3 resulted in 56% inhibition of TTR aggregation at 48 hr
source: At these concentrations, α1 and α3 resulted in 72 and 56% inhibition, respectively, relative to TTR alone at low pH.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The rc and β controls resulted in little to no inhibition of TTR aggregation
source: In contrast, the rc and β controls resulted in little to no inhibition.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The designs in the absence of TTR did not bind Congo red and were indistinguishable from the buffer-only controls
source: Moreover, the designs in the absence of TTR did not bind Congo red and were indistinguishable from the buffer-only controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: TTR toxicity was apparent around 24 hr of aggregation at pH 4.5
source: Toxicity was apparent around 24 hr, and the results from this time point are shown in Figure 2B.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Under aggregation conditions, the viability of SH-SY5Y cells treated with TTR was reduced by approximately 20%
source: Under these conditions, the viability of the treated cells was reduced by approximately 20%, indicating that TTR was aggregating via the toxic pathway.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2B

claim: α1 inhibited 81% of the remaining TTR aggregation when added to 24-hr pre-incubated, toxic TTR
source: However, when α1 and α3 were mixed with 24-hr pre-incubated, toxic TTR, they inhibited 81% and 77%, respectively, of the remaining TTR aggregation observed in the absence of inhibitor.
evidence: Based on experimental data from the aggregation assay

claim: α3 inhibited 77% of the remaining TTR aggregation when added to 24-hr pre-incubated, toxic TTR
source: However, when α1 and α3 were mixed with 24-hr pre-incubated, toxic TTR, they inhibited 81% and 77%, respectively, of the remaining TTR aggregation observed in the absence of inhibitor.
evidence: Based on experimental data from the aggregation assay

claim: α1 inhibited approximately 87% of Aβ fibril formation
source: Again α1 was more efficient, inhibiting approximately 87% of fibril formation compared with 66% for α3, when measured after the reaction stabilized at 22 hr.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2C

claim: α3 inhibited 66% of Aβ fibril formation
source: Again α1 was more efficient, inhibiting approximately 87% of fibril formation compared with 66% for α3, when measured after the reaction stabilized at 22 hr.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2C

claim: The β-sheet design resulted in 62% inhibition of Aβ fibrillization
source: The β-sheet design, β, also resulted in 62% inhibition of Aβ fibrillization, which began exerting its effect primarily between 0 and 6 hr.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2C

claim: α1 became inhibitory after Aβ aggregation proceeded for approximately 6 hr
source: In contrast, α1 became inhibitory after aggregation proceeded for approximately 6 hr.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2C

claim: The peptide designs alone did not alter the fluorescence of ThT
source: The peptide designs alone did not alter the fluorescence of ThT, and, as with Congo red, they were indistinguishable from buffer–only controls over the time course of the assay (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: Aβ toxicity reduced the viability of treated SH-SY5Y cells to less than 50% after 6 hr incubation
source: Aβ toxicity was also assessed using the MTT assay and found to reduce the viability of treated SH-SY5Y cells to less than 50% after 6 hr incubation (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Addition of α1 to a pre-aggregated (6 hr), toxic sample of Aβ showed essentially complete inhibition of 97%
source: Addition of the α-sheet designs to a pre-aggregated (6 hr), toxic sample of Aβ showed essentially complete inhibition of 97% for α1 and 96% for α3, compared with the extent of remaining aggregation observed in the absence of inhibitor.
evidence: Based on experimental data from the aggregation assay

claim: Addition of α3 to a pre-aggregated (6 hr), toxic sample of Aβ showed essentially complete inhibition of 96%
source: Addition of the α-sheet designs to a pre-aggregated (6 hr), toxic sample of Aβ showed essentially complete inhibition of 97% for α1 and 96% for α3, compared with the extent of remaining aggregation observed in the absence of inhibitor.
evidence: Based on experimental data from the aggregation assay

claim: All three immobilized α-sheet designs (α1, α2 and α3) bound significantly more TTR from pre-incubated, toxic oligomer-containing TTR solutions than did the rc and β controls
source: All three immobilized α-sheet designs (α1, α2 and α3) bound significantly more TTR from pre-incubated, toxic oligomer-containing TTR solutions (pre-incubated at low pH for 24 hr) than did the rc and β controls (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A

claim: The extent of TTR binding by the β and rc controls is the same as that of the column matrix alone
source: The extent of TTR binding by the β and rc controls is the same as that of the column matrix alone, which does bind some TTR in the absence of immobilized peptide (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: α1, α2 and α3 bound pre-aggregated, toxic Aβ preferentially, whereas β and rc did not
source: α1, α2 and α3 also bound pre-aggregated, toxic Aβ preferentially, whereas β and rc did not (Figure 3B, and see statistical analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: The β design preferentially bound fresh, monomeric Aβ solutions (0 hr) over the toxic solutions (6 hr)
source: In the case of the β design, it preferentially bound the fresh, monomeric Aβ solutions (0 hr) over the toxic solutions (6 hr) (Figure 3C)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C

claim: The β design inhibition of Aβ aggregation was due to interactions with the 'native' form, not the toxic oligomer
source: indicating that inhibition was due to interactions with the 'native' form, not the toxic oligomer.
evidence: Based on inference from the binding data shown in Figure 3C

claim: α1 did not bind native, tetrameric TTR nor fresh, monomeric Aβ but instead preferentially bound species from the toxic, aggregated 6 hr samples
source: In contrast, α-sheet, as demonstrated with α1, did not bind native, tetrameric TTR nor fresh, monomeric Aβ but instead preferentially bound species from the toxic, aggregated 6 hr samples (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3D

claim: The α-sheet designs did not bind the fibrillar forms of Aβ or TTR acquired by allowing the aggregation reactions to continue for over 3 weeks
source: Moreover, the α-sheet designs did not bind the fibrillar forms of Aβ or TTR acquired by allowing the aggregation reactions to continue for over 3 weeks, as illustrated with immobilized α1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4

claim: Mirror image structures formed by replacing whole L-amino acid sequences with D-amino acids produce mirror-image CD-spectra
source: Mirror image structures, formed by replacing whole L-amino acid sequences with D-amino acids, such as gramicidin A, produce mirror-image CD-spectra (Koeppe et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Koeppe et al., 1992

claim: The α-sheet structure would be effectively invisible in CD spectroscopy due to near equal absorbance of both left and right polarized light
source: We anticipate that the α-sheet structure would be effectively invisible due to near equal absorbance of both left and right polarized light, with any residual signal emanating from the turns and terminal residues.
evidence: Based on speculation about the expected CD properties of α-sheet

claim: Density functional theory calculations of α-sheet structures predict a strong high-frequency absorbance in the 1675–1680 cm−1 region, with a weaker band around 1640 cm−1
source: Torii recently performed density functional theory calculations of three slightly different orientations of α-sheet structures (Torii, 2008). All models featured a strong high-frequency absorbance in the 1675–1680 cm−1 region, with a weaker band around 1640 cm−1
evidence: Supported by citation to Torii, 2008

claim: The predicted FTIR signature of α-sheet appears to be distinct from α-helix (∼1650–1658 cm−1), β-sheet (∼1620–1640 cm−1) and turn structures (∼1670 cm−1)
source: which appears to be distinct from α-helix (∼1650–1658 cm−1), β-sheet (∼1620–1640 cm−1) and turn structures (∼1670 cm−1) (Barth and Zscherp, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barth and Zscherp, 2002

claim: Strong sequential dNN Nuclear Overhauser Effect crosspeaks are expected along the backbone of α-sheet due to the unique alignment of the amide groups
source: Owing to the unique alignment of the amide groups in an α-sheet, we expect to see strong sequential dNN Nuclear Overhauser Effect (NOE) crosspeaks along the backbone since the NH groups are aligned on one side of the chain instead of alternating between opposite faces as in β-sheet structure.
evidence: Based on speculation about expected NMR properties of α-sheet

claim: Long-range dNN or strong sequential dαN NOEs characteristic of β-sheets would not be expected in α-sheet
source: Furthermore, we would not expect to observe the long-range dNN or the strong sequential dαN NOEs characteristic of β-sheets.
evidence: Based on speculation about expected NMR properties of α-sheet

claim: The CD spectrum of rc shows a random coil signal with a strong negative absorption around 200 nm
source: The CD spectrum of rc shows a random coil signal with a strong negative absorption around 200 nm (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4A

claim: The rc peptide shows multiple small absorbance peaks in FTIR not corresponding to a predominance of any specific structure
source: In its FTIR spectrum we observe multiple small absorbance peaks not corresponding to a predominance of any specific structure (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4B

claim: β exhibits a CD spectrum reflective of β-structure and random coil, with a minimum near 220 nm and another near 200 nm
source: In agreement with previous structural work (Cochran et al., 2001a), β exhibits a CD spectrum reflective of β-structure and random coil, with a minimum near 220 nm and another near 200 nm (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cochran et al., 2001a and data shown in Figure 4A

claim: The β-sheet structure of β was confirmed by FTIR through its strong absorbance at 1632 cm−1
source: The β-sheet structure was confirmed by FTIR through its strong absorbance at 1632 cm−1 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4B

claim: The CD spectra for α1, α2 and α3 are essentially featureless, as expected for the cancellation of αL and αR signals, except for a slight dip around 200 nm consistent with turn formation
source: The CD spectra for α1, α2 and α3 are essentially featureless, as expected for the cancellation of αL and αR signals, except for a slight dip around 200 nm consistent with turn formation (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4A

claim: α1 and α2 exhibited the predicted FTIR α-sheet bands at 1640 and 1675–1680 cm−1
source: α1 and α2 exhibited the predicted FTIR α-sheet bands at 1640 and 1675–1680 cm−1 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4B

claim: The FTIR α-sheet bands were less pronounced in α3
source: These bands were less pronounced in α3.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Cyclization of the amide backbone of α3 through a non-optimal turn may have caused distortion of the structure
source: Cyclization of the amide backbone of α3 through a non-optimal turn may have caused distortion of the structure, as has been reported in other peptide systems (Clark et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citation to Clark et al., 2005 and inference from the FTIR data

claim: The designed α-sheet peptides do not form α-helix or β-sheet structure, and the random coil content is not large
source: Altogether, these results prove that the designed α-sheet peptides do not form α-helix or β-sheet structure, and that the random coil content is not large (compare against the scale of the rc control CD spectrum).
evidence: Based on inference from the CD and FTIR data

claim: Multiple sequential dNN NOEs were observed along the backbones of both α1 and α3
source: We performed further structural studies utilizing homonuclear NMR spectroscopy. Multiple sequential dNN NOEs were observed along the backbones of both α1 and α3 (α2 was not soluble enough for NMR) (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4C and 4D

claim: No long-range dNN or dαN NOEs indicative of α-helical or β-sheet structure were observed in α1 and α3
source: No long-range dNN or dαN NOEs indicative of α-helical or β-sheet structure (Wüthrich, 1986) were observed.
evidence: Supported by NMR data and citation to Wüthrich, 1986

claim: The calculated NH–NH distances in the strands are much shorter in the α-sheet compared to β-sheet, consistent with the strong dNN NOEs observed for both α1 and α3
source: The calculated NH–NH distances in the strands are much shorter in the α-sheet, consistent with the strong dNN NOEs observed for both α1 and α3
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The NMR data are consistent with α-sheet secondary structure and inconsistent with α-helix, random coil, and β-sheet structures
source: however, in support of the CD and FTIR spectroscopic data, the NMR data are consistent with α-sheet secondary structure and inconsistent with α-helix, random coil, and β-sheet structures.
evidence: Based on inference from the NMR data

claim: Ten years ago a common conformation was demonstrated among soluble oligomeric species from amyloid proteins/peptides of diverse sequence and structures that cross react with the A11 antibody
source: Ten years ago a common conformation was demonstrated among soluble oligomeric species from amyloid proteins/peptides of diverse sequence and structures that cross react with the A11 antibody (Kayed et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kayed et al., 2003

claim: The oligomers are conformationally heterogeneous
source: Unfortunately, the precise structure of this toxic intermediate remains elusive, and it has become clear that the oligomers are conformationally heterogeneous (Carulla et al., 2009; Bitan et al., 2005, and references therein).
evidence: Supported by citations to Carulla et al., 2009 and Bitan et al., 2005

claim: Three computationally derived α-sheet designs were synthesized and characterized experimentally, and they appear to adopt α-sheet structure
source: Three of these computationally derived designs were synthesized and characterized experimentally, and they do indeed appear to adopt α-sheet structure (as shown by FTIR, CD and NMR).
evidence: Based on the FTIR, CD, and NMR data presented

claim: The two soluble α-sheet designs (α1 and α3) inhibited both TTR and Aβ aggregation in solution
source: The two soluble α-sheet designs (α1 and α3) inhibited both TTR and Aβ aggregation in solution.
evidence: Based on the aggregation assay data presented in Figure 2

claim: When immobilized to agarose beads, all three α-sheet designs bound species from the toxic TTR and Aβ preparations preferentially over the nontoxic fresh samples
source: In addition, when immobilized to agarose beads, all three α-sheet designs bound species from the toxic TTR and Aβ preparations preferentially over the nontoxic fresh samples.
evidence: Based on the binding assay data presented in Figure 3

claim: The β control formed a β-hairpin and preferentially bound the monomeric form of Aβ and did not react with TTR
source: In contrast, the β control formed a β-hairpin, as supported by CD and FTIR, and it preferentially bound the monomeric form of Aβ and it did not react with TTR.
evidence: Based on the CD, FTIR, and binding assay data presented

claim: When mature fibrils were applied to the immobilized α-sheet designs, the fibrils did not bind and appeared to have no affinity for the α-sheet structure
source: When mature fibrils were applied to the immobilized α−sheet designs, the fibrils did not bind and appeared to have no affinity for the α-sheet structure.
evidence: Based on the binding assay data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 4

claim: The α-sheet peptides were not designed against a specific protein target, yet inhibition of aggregation was observed in two very different amyloid systems
source: While these α-sheet peptides were not designed against a specific protein target, we observed inhibition of aggregation in two very different amyloid systems.
evidence: Based on the experimental results showing inhibition in both TTR and Aβ systems

claim: These results support the hypothesis that α-sheet structure is involved in the toxic oligomeric stage of aggregation
source: These results support our hypothesis that α-sheet structure is involved in the toxic oligomeric stage of aggregation
evidence: Based on inference from all the experimental results presented

claim: The α-sheet designs may aid in capture of the elusive toxic oligomeric species for in-depth characterization
source: In addition, the α-sheet designs may aid in capture of the elusive toxic oligomeric species for in-depth characterization.
evidence: Based on speculation about potential applications of the α-sheet designs

claim: The α-sheet designs introduce a novel class of amyloid inhibitors that target the toxic soluble oligomeric state of different amyloidogenic peptides and proteins
source: Having demonstrated that the α-sheet structure may constitute a broad-based inhibitor of amyloidosis, our α-sheet designs introduce a novel class of amyloid inhibitors that target the toxic soluble oligomeric state of different amyloidogenic peptides and proteins.
evidence: Based on the experimental results showing inhibition in multiple amyloid systems

claim: At 0 ns, residues 105-121 of transthyretin form a β-hairpin
source: At 0 ns (top left) the residues of interest form a β-hairpin.
evidence: Supported by Figure 1A showing the structure at 0 ns

claim: After 30 ns of MD simulation, the β-sheet in transthyretin residues 105-121 has converted to an α-sheet
source: After 30 ns (top right) the β-sheet has converted to an α-sheet.
evidence: Supported by Figure 1A showing the structure at 30 ns

claim: The dihedral angles for residues 105-121 of transthyretin at 0 ns are found mainly in the β-region of the Ramachandran plot
source: The dihedral angles for 1 ns of dynamics of these residues are found mainly in the β-region of the Ramachandran plot (top left quadrant, lower left panel; increasing frequency of occupancy is shown from blue through red) with several turn residues in the αR conformation (bottom left quadrant).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1A showing the Ramachandran plot at 0 ns

claim: After 30 ns, the majority of residues 105-121 of transthyretin have moved from the β-region to the αL or αR region of the Ramachandran plot
source: The dihedral angles for 1 ns of dynamics of the same residues reveal that the majority of residues have moved from the β-region to the αL (top right quadrant) or αR region of the Ramachandran plot (lower right panel).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1A showing the Ramachandran plot at 30 ns

claim: Application of a TTR solution aggregated for 72 hr revealed the presence of small aggregates and fibrils
source: Application of a TTR solution aggregated for 72 hr revealed the presence of small aggregates and fibrils.
evidence: Supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2 showing AFM images

claim: Application of an aggregated Aβ solution reveals the presences of aggregates and fibrils
source: Application of an aggregated Aβ solution reveals the presences of aggregates and fibrils.
evidence: Supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 4 showing AFM images
